findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing blocklist bypass
findings.body: `should_block?` looks up the raw email with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, and the model's uniqueness validation is also exact. The User model does not normalize the email before the validator runs. On PostgreSQL, `bad@spam.com` and `Bad@Spam.com` are different values, so a blocked address can be used again simply by changing capitalization. Downcase the value for storage and lookup (for example with `Email.downcase`) and make uniqueness case-insensitive; otherwise the blocklist is trivially bypassable.

findings.title: Email validation mutates match statistics, so a blocked signup is counted twice
findings.body: This validator calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which increments `match_count` and saves the record. `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save` on the same user. For a blocked address both calls run this validator, so one signup attempt increments `match_count` twice, and any repeated `valid?` call also writes to the database. Validation should be side-effect free; record the match when the rejection is actually handled, or otherwise ensure it is counted once.

findings.title: match_count update is a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1; record.save` loses updates when concurrent validations hit the same blocked email: two requests can read the same count and both write the same incremented value. Since this counter is meant to track how often the blocklist matches, use an atomic update such as `increment_counter`/`update_counters` (plus `update_column` for `last_match_at`) rather than saving the model after reading the value into Ruby.

findings.title: Domain whitelist regex is not anchored, allowing whitelist bypass
findings.body: `email_in_restriction_setting?` builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` and uses `value =~ regexp`, so it matches an allowed domain anywhere after `@`. With a whitelist of `example.com`, `user@example.com.attacker.net` matches and is accepted even though its real domain is not whitelisted; the blacklist has the same suffix-matching problem in reverse. Anchor the domain at the end of the address (and escape the configured domains) so whitelist/blacklist checks compare the actual domain.

findings.title: Validator specs stub the blocklist and do not cover the real paths
findings.body: Both examples stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so they do not exercise the real blocklist record, case normalization, the returned `user.email.blocked` message, or the whitelist/blacklist logic that was moved into this new validator. A regression in those shipping paths would still pass these specs. Add coverage using real `BlockedEmail` records, mixed-case addresses, and at least one whitelist/blacklist case.
